claims.claim: ATI occupies a materials/process bottleneck in aerospace, defense and specialty energy: nickel superalloys, titanium alloys, forgings and advanced powders connect constrained metallurgical capacity to jet engines, airframes and defense systems.

The structural advantage is scenario-robust only while qualification barriers, process know-how and capacity scarcity persist; successor bottlenecks can shift toward customer qualification, furnace ramp execution, raw-material availability or alternative material/process architectures.

causalEdges: aerospace/defense production -> demand for high-performance qualified materials -> ATI melting/forging/alloy capacity
materials science + qualification barriers -> constrained qualified supply -> pricing/contract leverage
capacity expansion -> customer qualification -> usable supply growth -> backlog conversion

risks.risk: Capacity is valuable only after qualification; ramp delays or cost overruns can postpone conversion of scarcity into cash flow.

unknowns.unknown: Long-run substitution rates from alternative materials or manufacturing routes are not quantified in current evidence.

claims.claim: Aerospace and defense represented 69% of ATI year-to-date sales, so the same end-market strength supporting the thesis also creates concentration and cycle/program exposure.

Q2 margin and guidance strength reduce near-term execution concern, but new-facility qualification costs and a facility-sale gain mean headline earnings should not be treated as frictionless evidence of capacity-ramp economics.

risks.risk: End-market concentration raises sensitivity to aerospace build rates, defense programs and customer qualification schedules.
Expansion economics can disappoint if new furnaces/facilities qualify slowly or carry structurally higher manufacturing costs.

unknowns.unknown: Customer-level concentration and contract repricing protections require deeper source-addressed underwriting.
